Sampling subgroups

Source: vignettes/sampling.Rmd
sampling.Rmd
library(retrogroup)

vignette("model", package = "retrogroup") derives \(p_{ik}\), an estimate of the posterior probability that patient \(i\) belongs to subgroup level \(k\) (\(i = 1, \ldots, n\), \(k = 1, \ldots, K\)). This vignette explains a method to sample subgroup levels \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\) given fixed posterior probability estimates \(p_{ik}\).

Over a large number of simulations, subgroup log hazard ratios computed on the simulated datasets should match the published log hazard ratios on average. However, each individual simulated dataset is subject to random variation and may not exactly match the published statistics. vignette("optimization", package = "retrogroup") defines methods to refine an individual dataset so the observed and published subgroup log hazard ratios match.

Unconstrained sampling

If we treat subgroup levels as unconstrained, each \(x_i\) has its own independent categorical distribution with probabilities \(p_{i1}, \ldots, p_{iK}\). Independently for each patient \(i = 1, \ldots, n\), we draw:

\[ x_i \sim \text{Categorical}(p_{i1}, \ldots, p_{iK}) \]

Unconstrained sampling is simple, but it does not guarantee that the resulting subgroup assignments match \(n_k\), the published number of patients in each subgroup level \(k\) from vignette("framing", package = "retrogroup"). For that, we need constrained sampling.

Constrained sampling

Constrained sampling forces the sampled subgroup levels to match the published counts \(n_k\) for each subgroup level \(k\). To preserve the counts, we iterate through a random permutation of patients and assign each one to a random subgroup level with fewer than \(n_k\) patients.

Let \(\rho_1, \ldots, \rho_n\) be a random permutation of patient indexes \(1, \ldots, n\). Every \(n_k\) is strictly positive, so every subgroup level has room for the first patient, and we draw \(x_{\rho_1}\) from a categorical distribution:

\[ x_{\rho_1} \sim \text{Categorical}(p_{{\rho_1}1}, \ldots, p_{{\rho_1}K}) \]

At arbitrary patient \(\rho_j\), patients \(\rho_1, \ldots, \rho_{j-1}\) have already been assigned to subgroup levels, with \(n^*_{jk} := \sum_{h = 1}^{j - 1} I(x_{\rho_h} = k)\) patients in subgroup level \(k\) so far. We draw \(x_{\rho_j}\) from a categorical distribution that excludes subgroup levels that have already reached their published counts:

\[ x_{\rho_j} \sim \text{Categorical}(q_{{\rho_j}1}, \ldots, q_{{\rho_j}K}) \]

where:

\[ q_{{\rho_j}k} := \begin{cases} \dfrac{p_{{\rho_j}k}}{\sum_{l = 1}^K I(n^*_{jl} < n_l) p_{{\rho_j}l}}, & \text{if } n^*_{jk} < n_k \\ 0, & \text{if } n^*_{jk} = n_k \end{cases} \]

We assume \(\sum_{k = 1}^K n_k = n\), so at least one subgroup level has room at every step. Every \(p_{ik}\) is strictly positive, as shown in vignette("model", package = "retrogroup"), so the denominator above is positive. This scheme guarantees the published counts, but it is only an approximate draw from independent categorical distributions conditional on those counts, because patients late in the permutation can only join subgroup levels that still have room.
